lines: Progressive irritation, persistent itching, and skin changes of external genitalia over 7 months

She has tried various lubricants and estrogen creams prescribed by a different provider, with little to no relief.
She has also noticed that the area around her vaginal opening has changed in appearance, with loss of definition and increasing sensitivity.

encounters.cc: Severe crushing chest pain and diaphoresis consistent with acute myocardial infarction

lines: Severe crushing chest pain and diaphoresis consistent with acute myocardial infarction
This 73-year-old with constipation and hiatal hernia presents to ICU.
Her family reports she often complained of left lower quadrant abdominal discomfort.
- Postmenopausal status (menopause at age 51, no hormone replacement therapy)
The patient’s past medical history is significant for long-standing constipation, for which she frequently used laxatives.
She also had a 25-year history of hypertension.
She had been hospitalized once for an episode of diverticulitis five years prior.
She was treated with antibiotics at that time, with full recovery.
- Acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours PRN pain
- Polyethylene glycol 3350 17 g daily PRN constipation
Her social history is notable for frequent international travel.
As a young adult, she spent two years working in rural India as a volunteer teacher.
Later in life, she worked as a travel journalist, visiting multiple countries across Africa, South America, and Europe.
She wrote extensively about public health conditions in different parts of the world.
Her occupations included teaching, writing, and later serving as a tour guide.
Despite these varied experiences, she had no history of parasitic infection or tropical illness.
Her dietary history included frequent consumption of refined, low-fiber foods while traveling.
She often joked with her family that her “Western diet” was easier to maintain abroad than local diets.
Her physicians had repeatedly encouraged her to increase her dietary fiber, but she often ignored this advice.
She worked at a desk for long stretches when writing, which contributed to her sedentary lifestyle.
An autopsy is performed to evaluate the extent of her coronary artery disease and to document other comorbidities.
Her heart is found to have severe atherosclerotic narrowing of all three major coronary arteries.
The left anterior descending artery has a 95% occlusion with evidence of thrombus formation.
The posterior descending artery has moderate narrowing.
The myocardium shows a large area of transmural infarction.
In addition to the cardiac findings, several other organs are examined.
The lungs show mild emphysematous changes, likely related to her history of tobacco use.
Her liver is mildly steatotic, which her physicians had attributed to long-standing obesity.
The uterus and ovaries are atrophic, consistent with her postmenopausal age.
When the pathologist examines the large intestine, an additional abnormality is noted.
The sigmoid colon appears irregular and somewhat thickened.
Careful inspection reveals multiple small, round outpouchings ranging from 0.5 to 1 cm.
These outpouchings are located along the antimesenteric border between the teniae coli.
They are filled with inspissated stool and are surrounded by hypertrophied smooth muscle bands.
On closer examination, it is clear that these lesions represent herniations of mucosa and submucosa through the muscular layer.
Microscopy of one of these lesions shows attenuated colonic mucosa, with no evidence of epithelial dysplasia or malignant transformation.
The muscularis propria is intact but interrupted at the site of the pouch, where the mucosa protrudes.
At autopsy, these sigmoid lesions are carefully documented.
The pathologist notes that they are not true diverticula because they do not involve all layers of the bowel wall.
Instead, they consist only of mucosa and submucosa herniating through areas of weakness in the muscularis propria.
No evidence of carcinoma or polypoid lesions is found in the colon.
